title: Om, the essence of essences
hookLine: year two opens the Chandogya Upanishad, and its very first line says: meditate on om, the high chant
tomorrow: speech and breath argue about who is greatest

lines: A FIRE, A CIRCLE OF PRIESTS.
cards: Year two opens beside a fire. In the old Vedic sacrifice, priests sit around a fire on an altar, each with a job. One pours the offerings.
One recites the verses. And one, the singer, waits for his moment, then lifts his voice into a long, rising chant: the udgitha, the high song. It was his whole craft.
Now suppose someone in that circle asked a strange question. Not how do you sing it, but what is it, really? What is the song made of?
The Chandogya Upanishad, where year two begins, opens with an answer.

teach.h: THE VEDA OF CHANTS BEGINS WITH A SONG.
teach.b: The Chandogya belongs to the Sama Veda, the Veda of chants, so of course it starts with singing. Its first words are om ity etad aksharam udgitham upasita. Roughly: meditate on this syllable, om, as the udgitha.

teach.h: OM AND THE HIGH SONG ARE ONE.
teach.b: The high song and the sacred syllable are one. Then the text builds a ladder of essences. The essence of all these beings is the earth.

teach.h: A LADDER: EARTH TO WATER TO PERSON.
teach.b: Of earth, water. Of water, plants. Of plants, the human person.
Of the person, speech. Of speech, the verses of the Rig Veda. Of the verses, the chant of the Sama Veda.
And the essence of the chant is the udgitha, which is om.
Then comes the line the whole day turns on: the udgitha is rasanam rasatamah, the essence of essences, the highest, the eighth rung. Rasa means juice, sap, flavor, the best part of a thing.
Follow it down again: soil, rain, rice, a person, a voice, a verse, a song, a single syllable. In the text's picture, a person, boiled down, ends in a sound.
That's the Upanishad's move, and you'll see it all year: it takes something the priests already did, a song at a fire, and asks what it means on the inside. The ritual stays. The meaning goes deeper.
Om still opens prayer, study and puja in Hindu homes and temples today, and this chapter is one place that asks why.

how: Many Hindus chant om at the start and end of prayer, study and puja; in traditional Vedic schools, students of the Sama Veda still learn the Chandogya's chants by ear from a teacher.

o: the high chant of the Sama Veda, which the text calls om
the fire the priests pour offerings into at the altar
the opening verse of the Rig Veda, recited first

games.q: the ladder of essences — tap the pairs.
p: the verses of the Rig Veda

s: the Chandogya Upanishad belongs to the Sama Veda
the Veda of chants. that's why it opens with the singer's high song.
the Upanishad tells the priests to stop the ritual
it keeps the ritual and asks what it means on the inside.
rasa means juice, sap or essence
the best part of a thing. the udgitha is the essence of essences.

games.q: you're a priest who has sung the high chant at the fire your whole life. someone asks what the song is really made of. what does the Chandogya answer?
o: it's just a melody; don't overthink it.
it's om, the essence at the top of a ladder of essences.
it's a secret only kings may hear.
games.why: the first line says to meditate on om as the udgitha, then traces a ladder from earth to water to person to speech to song, ending in om.

practice: Climb the ladder in your mind: the ground under you, the water you drank today, the food it grew, your body made from that food, your voice.
If you'd like, let one soft om come out on the breath, or simply hear it inside, and notice it begin, swell and fade. Then rest in the quiet after it, the way the text rests at the top of its ladder.

wordCard.voice: The udgitha. The high song of the Sama Veda priests, which the Chandogya identifies with om and calls the essence of essences.

orig.note: Sanskrit udgītha: the high chant sung by the Sama Veda priest. the Chandogya's first line identifies it with om.

carryVoice: Your line: om, the essence of essences. Boil a prayer down and this is what's left, so it comes first. Year two has begun.
